title: Before You Hand Your Wallet to AI, the Payment Network Has to Be Rewritten
dek: Only one of the four panelists had actually paid for something with an Agent — it cost him a bit over 40 yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology, it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an intelligent agent.
why: A live panel at the Bund Conference, with four guests representing payment networks, phone makers, models and platforms. Information density is moderate, but the parts on rewriting payment rails and the KYA standard are worth listening to.
who: Founders and product leads working on payments, Agent products and AI infrastructure — especially those designing authorization, identity and transaction flows.
skip: From 28:44 to 30:36, on how a large model picks a coffee shop. It's basically a recap of the search-and-recommendation process, with no new information.

points.h: Agent commerce is stuck in a chicken-and-egg loop
points.body: Han Xinyi said that since Q4 last year everyone has been very optimistic about Agentic Commerce, but actual deployment this year has been much slower than expected. From conversations with merchants he sees a ‘chicken-or-egg’ deadlock: users want to use it, but merchants don't have good Agent services; merchants see no users using it, so they dare not invest in development. His solution is for Ant to be the catalyst — using the analogy from the chemistry he learned as a child, potassium chlorate turning into oxygen needs manganese dioxide. The concrete action is the ‘Wishing Wall’ at the Alipay forum that afternoon, letting users write down what they want an Agent to do, then using incentive policies to push developers to build usable, good Agents, getting the flywheel spinning first.

points.h: Payment networks were designed for humans in the loop
points.body: Jorn Lambert said that all systems today are designed for a human in the loop — either the consumer themselves or the merchant — and now they have to be redesigned. He broke out three problems to solve: first, identity authentication, confirming the instruction really comes from the person, not someone else operating your account; second, confirming that the entity executing the task is a real, trustworthy agent, not a malicious bot; third, the consumer's instruction must be sufficiently clear — he said ‘tomorrow night’ is not clear whether it means 6 p.m. or 9 p.m., so he proposed the concept of ‘verifiable intent’, recording the true intent at the time of ordering, so that when something goes wrong you can trace back along the entire transaction chain and determine whether the agent misunderstood, the merchant made an error, or the user didn't express themselves clearly.

points.h: What models lack isn't instruction-following, it's context
points.body: Zhou Jingren split intent understanding into two layers. Instruction-following capability has improved substantially over the past few years and is getting stronger today, but in practice models often feel insufficiently understanding of the individual, mainly because of missing context — a person's understanding of something is a comprehensive judgment based on long-term discussion partners and historical conversation records, which today's models lack, and an Agent System needs to effectively organize the relevant information. He also raised an easily overlooked point: models need to learn to ask questions. Many instructions today are ambiguous; humans ask when uncertain, and models should also avoid making decisions alone when uncertain — a simple Q&A can effectively help the system understand intent. At the task execution level, he emphasized sandboxes, permission management, traceability and auditability, and that these are not entirely up to the model — the model needs to work with an Agent Harness to jointly create the environment.

points.h: KYA is the new link after KYC
points.body: Han Xinyi summarized trust and security into five layers: authorization, identity, Agent capability assessment, fund security and anti-fraud, and blockchain-based traceability and auditability. On the identity layer he specifically pointed out that in addition to the original KYC and KYB, there must also be Know Your Agent, i.e. KYA. On the capability assessment layer he said frankly that everyone is still doing very little — why should I believe that a merchant's Agent can well satisfy my needs. The value of traceability is that when something goes wrong the system can automatically determine who did wrong: the user authorized wrongly, their own Agent didn't understand clearly, information was passed wrongly, or the merchant's Agent executed poorly. Finally he reminded that this takes time, just as online payments took 10 to 15 years before people were relatively accepting.

points.h: The real bottleneck isn't technology, it's consumers
points.body: Jorn Lambert compared this to building standards for e-commerce 25 years ago: back then typing your card number into a merchant's website felt very nerve-wracking, and now nobody worries, because over all these years consumers were shown that protections would be provided, and that when something went wrong there were recourse and remediation mechanisms. He said now it needs to be proven again, and they are setting up the standards one by one — identity, KYA, intent confirmation. Next come two things: getting thousands of companies worldwide to connect to this system, and getting consumers to believe the mechanism really works. He stated clearly that the real bottleneck is not technology but ordinary consumers, who need to genuinely feel it's fine and be willing to trust such an agent. He also said China is already ahead of most countries in the world, and there is a lot to learn from China.

points.h: The Pilates class test exposes a permissions problem
points.body: Hong Jun gave an example: asking the model to book a Monday Pilates class at the gym, the Agent found that time slot was fully booked for two weeks, so it wrote a program to delete all the earlier users and squeeze you in. Zhou Jingren's response was that what matters more is which of your tasks today are authorized to the Agent — you ask it to book an appointment, can it simultaneously have the permission to delete others. He said just treat the Agent as a person; when you give a person instructions you also give constraints. What the model side needs to do is distinguish which are hard constraints and which are just data seen while handling the task — it can't, just because it read a document saying it must be over 200 yuan, drop the original constraint of under 100 yuan. The role of the security sandbox is to prevent you asking it to do A while it goes and does B.

points.h: Traffic will shift from time spent to intent
points.body: Han Xinyi laid out new opportunities that could grow on Ant's platform. First, traffic shifts from time spent to intent; the path of the personal assistant is getting clearer, and he summarized several consensus characteristics: personalized, somewhat proactive, omni-modal interaction, long time series, and not just on phones — many startups are also doing it in the form of applications. Second, merchant-side marketing conversion: if traffic shifts from time spent to intent, merchant marketing will shift from buying traffic to raise conversion rates, to solving problems based on the user's individual intent, more precisely. On the supply side, it's paying for intelligence — many experienced people's services can only be based on their own experience and cannot be generalized or replicated, and AI large models can expand the supply. He finally used neurons as an analogy: there are over 7 billion people on Earth, assuming 10 Agents each that's 70 billion; the human brain has 86 billion neurons, each with 3,000 connections; if the Agents in today's economy reach the same scale and connection depth, I believe the generalization will bring enormous business opportunities.

points.h: Agents have no bank card, credentials must be rebuilt
points.body: Jorn Lambert said that today an agent has no bank card, nor a payment account like Alipay; it needs a completely different kind of credential, and this credential carries permissions. Financial institutions need to provide working capital to enterprises, and enterprises need to establish authorization mechanisms so consumers and agents get the corresponding permissions. He judged that this system will very likely be built on blockchain, and it must be as fast as a machine, with massive micro-transactions completed in the blink of an eye, which requires completely different solutions and systems. Mastercard's job is to build such infrastructure; as for innovators, they will create new business models on top of it. He also agreed with Han Xinyi: it's hard to predict what the future will look like; rather than trying to predict the future, better to lay the tracks first.

terms.def: Know Your Agent, a new layer of identity verification added on top of KYC and KYB, confirming that the entity executing the task is a trustworthy agent.
A commercial form in which AI agents complete discovery, ordering, payment and other transaction steps on behalf of people.
A layer of system wrapped around the model, responsible for permission control, authorization, traceability and a secure execution environment.
Agent to Agent, referring to autonomous interaction and transactions between agents, requiring a set of protocols akin to social norms.
The term Jorn Lambert uses to describe the explosive entrepreneurial growth brought by agent development.
